story: Itzamná was an upper god of the sky, regarded as a creator deity. He was invoked in yearly rituals: in one month a ritual sprinkling of sacred books was performed in his honor as 'the first priest'; in another he was called on as a god of medicine; and in a further month the very old venerated him alongside the rain deities. One year in a four-year cycle was placed under his patronage. Itzamná was credited with inventing the priestly art of writing. He was said to have once been a priestly figure who divided the land and gave names to all its features. He was regarded as the creator of humankind and as father of a fourfold deity dwelling in the interior of the earth. In another tradition, he fathered thirteen sons with a goddess, two of whom created the earth and humankind. In pictorial scenes he could be shown clinging to the back of a peccary or a deer, held ready for sacrifice, or shot at while in the form of a bird. He was also shown seated on a celestial throne, governing agriculture and the hunt. His head sometimes appeared within the jaws of a two-headed caiman representing the earth, seen as his transformation in a creation account. He could take the shape of a great bird that carried a two-headed serpent in its beak, associated with rain; this bird was one of four such spirits seated atop four world trees, re-erected after the sky once collapsed. Its shooting was a major episode in a twin heroes' myth. Human rulers took his name as part of their titles, and in one scene a dignitary wearing his bird form's headdress bestowed a royal headband upon a king, acting as the creator god granting rulership.
